name: 担担麺 胡 YEBISU 円町店 (Tantanmen Yebisu (Ebisu) Enmachi-ten)

claims.text: This is a wheat-noodle ramen kitchen; tantanmen noodles and soy-based seasonings contain wheat, with no gluten-free accommodation indicated, so heavy gluten cross-contact is expected.
No wheat-free tamari indicated; standard Japanese wheat-containing soy sauce should be assumed.

The kitchen primarily prepares meat tantanmen alongside the single vegan tofu bowl, so shared surfaces and utensils mean possible animal cross-contact; the vegan dish itself is formulated without animal ingredients per VegeMap.
No specific allergy-handling protocol is published; VegeMap recommends consulting staff before ordering regarding dietary restrictions.
The vegetable tantanmen is intentionally built as a vegan dish, with Kyoto tofu instead of minced meat and a broth with no animal ingredients.

Standard Japanese soy sauce and miso glazes used in shojin ryori typically contain wheat; the restaurant does not advertise wheat-free seasonings, so strict-GF diners should confirm in advance. (General shojin/Japanese cuisine norm; not specifically stated by the venue.)
The kitchen is fully plant-based — no animal-based ingredients are used at all ('動物性の素材を一切使用せず') — so there is no meat or fish cross-contact in the kitchen.
Meals are reservation-based by phone (075-882-9725, 9:00–17:00), giving an opportunity to communicate allergies or dietary needs ahead of the visit; no formal allergy-handling program is published.

Entirely vegan kitchen: a temple-run shojin ryori operation that uses zero animal products, with plant-based (kombu/seaweed) dashi rather than fish dashi — eliminating dairy, egg, meat and fish cross-contact concerns.
Set-course format with consistent, well-documented dishes (sesame tofu, yuba, simmered seasonal vegetables) makes it easy to know what you are eating.

name: ザ・リッツ・カールトン京都 (The Ritz-Carlton, Kyoto)

claims.text: Guests are asked to inform their server of any food allergies or vegetarian/vegan needs so the kitchen can accommodate them; allergy disclosure before ordering is part of the standard service.
La Locanda's menu clearly labels vegan (VG), gluten-free (GF) and lactose-free (LF) dishes, so diners can identify safe options instead of guessing.
A locally made, 100% gluten-free amazake granola is offered at breakfast, indicating genuine gluten-free sourcing awareness.
English-speaking, professionally trained luxury-hotel staff make it straightforward to communicate and customize dietary requests.
The entire menu is built around fu, which is concentrated wheat gluten, so the kitchen is inherently wheat-heavy and not suitable for gluten-avoidant or celiac diners.
No wheat-free soy sauce was confirmed; standard Japanese soy sauce and seasonings typically contain wheat.
Default broth/dashi is not confirmed vegan; a vegan-friendly soup stock must be requested at least three days in advance and cannot be arranged same-day.
The restaurant will accommodate a vegan broth if notified at least three days ahead, indicating they handle dietary requests with advance notice.
Core dishes are plant-based fu (wheat gluten) and yuba (tofu skin) in the shojin vegetarian tradition, so the menu is largely free of meat and fish.

name: 野菜ダイニング 薬師 (Yasai Dining Kusushi)

claims.text: This is an omnivore izakaya, not a vegan kitchen: the regular menu includes dairy (cheese bakes, cheese-topped pizza) and the kitchen handles meat and fish, so a vegan order shares equipment and surfaces with animal products. Vegan dishes are prepared only on advance request, so cross-contact handling depends entirely on arranging this ahead.

The vegan map listing states vegan service is available 'by advance reservation,' implying the kitchen will tailor a plant-based course if you call ahead (075-212-4313) - but no formal allergen or gluten protocol is published.
The whole concept is vegetable-forward, so plant-based diners have a genuinely large palette of seasonal Kyoto and nationwide vegetables to draw from when a vegan course is arranged in advance.

No information published on whether the soy sauce or miso used is wheat-free; standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat, so gluten-sensitive diners should assume wheat is present unless they confirm otherwise.
Japan VegeMap classifies the cafe as fully vegan (飲食店（全てヴィーガン）), meaning the kitchen uses no meat, seafood, eggs, dairy, or honey — so animal cross-contact risk is inherently low across the menu.
Fully plant-based kitchen, so the entire menu is suitable for vegans and no animal-derived ingredients are used.
Macrobiotic/grain-based cooking centered on rice and seasonal vegetables, with simple, whole-food preparations.
VegeMap advises informing staff about dietary requirements before ordering, as the listing is unverified and offerings may differ from what is shown.
The shop's signature offering is described as gluten- and dairy-free doughnuts alongside house-roasted coffee, indicating a deliberate focus on gluten-free and dairy-free baking.

name: DOON Shokudo Indosan (DOON食堂 印度山)

claims.text: Shop states all curries are gluten-free; served with rice (no naan on menu). Shared home kitchen — confirm no wheat-thickened item and clean serving.
North Indian curries; soy sauce not typical, but confirm no wheat/hing-with-wheat in any dish.
Bean curry is vegan-compatible; chicken curry uses halal chicken — confirm ghee/dairy separation for strict vegans.
Own statement: all curries gluten-free, nut-free, sugar-free, no MSG; featured on a wheat-allergy blogger's Matsumoto GF tour.
Every curry is gluten-, nut-, sugar- and MSG-free by the shop's own claim, with rice — a reliable curry-and-rice option.
